Louisiana Delays Full DraftKings License Over AI Concerns

Published October 21, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The Louisiana Gaming Control Board declined to grant DraftKings a standard license renewal at a hearing this week, instead approving only a conditional extension while it investigates reports that the operator uses artificial intelligence to target losing bettors and manage VIP customers who may be showing signs of a gambling problem.

What the board decided

DraftKings' Louisiana sports betting license was set to expire Nov. 10. Rather than renew it outright, the board voted unanimously to conditionally extend the license through Feb. 19, with a full renewal hearing now scheduled for Feb. 18. Board chairman Chris Hebert said the move isn't a finding of wrongdoing: "Rather, it is a measured regulatory response that allows us as a board to fulfill our oversight responsibilities," he said, while also noting that "a news report, or news reports, plural, are not findings of regulatory violations."

The conditional extension comes with a list of requirements, including formal written responses within 30 days to questions about DraftKings' use of artificial intelligence and prediction-market activity, a compliance review of its responsible-gambling marketing materials, monthly compliance reports starting on the 15th of each month, and resolution of an outstanding shareholder suitability check that the board said it also needs more time to complete.

DraftKings pushes back

Company president and co-founder Paul Liberman told the board DraftKings doesn't use AI to single out particular customers or segments for targeting, framing the platform's business as entertainment rather than pursuit of losing bettors: "We don't use that, once again, to target in any way a particular customer or customer segment because we don't think that that's relevant." Chief Responsible Gaming Officer Lori Kalani said the company does use automated tools to flag customers who may need help, but drew a line on diagnosis: "We can't diagnose when someone has a compulsive gambling problem. We're not physicians, we're not clinicians."

DraftKings also disclosed it has closed 175 Louisiana accounts so far this year for responsible-gambling reasons, which Kalani said is tracking similar to 2025's pace.

Why it matters

This is the second state this month where DraftKings has faced direct regulatory questions about AI-driven marketing and VIP management — Massachusetts regulators recently asked operators industry-wide whether their AI tools target losing bettors. Louisiana's conditional-renewal approach, rather than an outright denial, suggests regulators are treating this as an open compliance question rather than a settled violation, but it signals that AI-assisted marketing and VIP programs are becoming a live regulatory flashpoint nationally, not just a Louisiana-specific issue. Bettors in Louisiana can continue to use DraftKings without interruption under the conditional license; the practical story to watch is what the board's investigation turns up before the Feb. 18 hearing.
